items.title: Earl Turbinton Interview, 1990-09-01
items.q: during the later part when he was in high school i used him in my band

ctx.x: if you're involved in the evolution of a music, then naturally you would have to go back and study the music from its inception or from its very beginning and find out what all the masters that came before, so that you would have a chronological insight, a chronological appreciation from a student's standpoint to know the lineage of the drummers, the lineage of the soprano, saxophone players, clarinetists, and so on through all the instruments, and to see how what we were playing at that time, which was often…

jolt to the jazz community and it kind of inspired musicians to play even though excuse me even though there was um a lot of uh sometimes hostility towards the sort of new music we knew that we had to keep on forging ahead and i think it helped to inspire guys to go on their gigs and play more creative music to try to find some jazz outlets and that was also a period that they had these late night jam sessions and there were several black clubs that were vibrant then that aren't vibrant now there were there were…
you need a break yeah for a minute
